clue.text: Refuse to agree to project

blocks.note: first meaning: to hold out against others and decline to go along
second meaning: to jut out or protrude

explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' reads as a noun, a scheme someone refuses to back, but here it is the verb meaning to stick out.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both holding firm in dissent and physically protruding beyond a surface.

clue.text: Yes, truly an inspiration

blocks.note: yea is an old word meaning indeed or truly
H is the breathed sound, the aspirate, so one intake of breath

explanation.surface: Someone agrees enthusiastically, calling an idea a real inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: H is called the aspirate because it is pronounced as a breath, hence 'an inspiration'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the casual spoken form of agreement, an informal variant of the plain affirmative.

clue.text: Great influence of one politician on some legislation

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
Member of Parliament
an act is a piece of legislation

explanation.surface: A single politician has had a big effect on a piece of law-making.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong effect or marked influence on something is commonly described with this noun.

clue.text: King surrounded by subjects in sunny region

indicators.note: being surrounded means sitting inside the other word, so the king goes within the subjects

blocks.note: R for Rex, Latin for king
subjects of discussion

explanation.surface: A monarch among his loyal subjects in some sun-drenched colony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subjects' suggests a king's people, but here they are subjects of conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: The hot belt of the earth either side of the equator gets strong year-round sunshine.

clue.text: Safe vessel, one showing no sign of age

definitions.text: one showing no sign of age

blocks.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
a pan is a cooking vessel

explanation.surface: A strongbox and a container, and a person who never seems to get older.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter is underworld slang for a safe (a safecracker was a peterman), a convention worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's boy who never grows up lends his name to anyone who stays youthful forever.

clue.text: Cheerless accommodation booked by Dickens

definitions.note: describes the novel rather than naming it: a title written up in a book by Dickens

blocks.note: bleak means dreary and cheerless
a house provides accommodation

explanation.surface: Gloomy lodgings that were reserved by the novelist himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booked' looks like a reservation, as for a hotel room, but means put into a book.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of the 1853 novel by Charles Dickens about the Jarndyce lawsuit.

clue.text: It cuts things rather fine

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who leaves barely enough time or margin
setter's reading: a kitchen machine that chops meat into very small pieces

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting it fine' is an idiom for leaving little time; here it is literal chopping.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen appliance that grinds meat finely is exactly a device that cuts things small.

clue.text: Flagship rounds end of pier

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter only
to round something is to go about it, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: a steamer is a steam-powered ship
last letter of pier

explanation.surface: The lead ship of a fleet sails round the tip of a jetty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flagship' looks like one word, but it splits into the definition 'Flag' and 'ship'.
explanation.definitionFit: A long narrow flag or pennant flown from a mast is a streamer.

clue.text: Cake made by Claire

indicators.note: something made is put together from raw material, so the name is reworked

blocks.note: the name taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A woman named Claire did some baking.
explanation.definitionFit: A choux pastry finger filled with cream and topped with chocolate is a classic small cake.

clue.text: It doesnÍt go far in church

blocks.note: taken as written
CH is the standard abbreviation for church; that the letters also run straight through 'in church' is a coincidence of the charade, not a hidden word

explanation.surface: Something or someone that makes little headway inside a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny unit of length, about two and a half centimetres, covers very little distance.

clue.text: Served with pork? Nonsense!

blocks.note: first meaning: the fruit condiment traditionally eaten with roast pork
second meaning: old American slang for rubbish or claptrap

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation makes it sound like a diner scoffing at a menu; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both the sweet fruit accompaniment to roast meat and dated slang for insincere talk or humbug.

clue.text: Doctor in habit of fighting

indicators.note: one item placed in another means it sits within that other word

blocks.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, a medical degree
a habit is a garment, as is a coat

explanation.surface: A physician who is in the habit of picking fights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the habit of' reads as an idiom, but habit here is clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Armed fighting between forces is called combat, a noun for battle or conflict.

clue.text: Office worker disliked by librarians?

blocks.note: surface reading: a clerk who keeps an office's accounts
setter's reading: someone who keeps borrowed volumes and never returns them

explanation.walkthrough: Read the compound literally: a person who keeps the library's books, the bane of librarians.
explanation.definitionFit: An accounts clerk who records financial transactions holds this job title in many offices.

clue.text: Chaperon needed going round place with a rough reputation

indicators.note: going round suggests turning and moving about, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A young woman of doubtful reputation needs a chaperon when going about town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough reputation' hints at a person; it means rough seas.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern tip of South America is notorious among sailors for storms and heavy seas.

clue.text: A prize for waste

blocks.note: taken as written
a trophy is a prize

explanation.surface: An award handed out for squandering things.
explanation.definitionFit: To atrophy is to waste away, as muscles do when unused; verb matches verb.

clue.text: Tear shed in a pillow, perhaps

indicators.note: to shed is to cast off and scatter, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter, the indicator doing double duty

explanation.surface: Someone weeps into their pillow.
explanation.definitionFit: A pillow is one example of a cushion that supports the back of someone lying or sitting.

clue.text: Misery that comes out in a gush

indicators.note: what comes out pours forth in a jumble, so the letters emerge in another order

blocks.note: the three words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Pent-up unhappiness that suddenly bursts out in a flood of tears.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe mental suffering or distress is a close synonym for deep misery.

clue.text: Main source of strength for a nation

definitions.text: Main source of strength for a nation

blocks.clueFragment: Main source of strength for a nation
blocks.note: surface reading: the chief thing that makes a country strong
setter's reading: the main is the ocean, so strength drawn from the ocean

explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like an adjective meaning chief; in crosswords and poetry it is the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A navy and merchant fleet give a country naval strength, the capacity to control the oceans.

clue.text: Middle-aged English travel writer

blocks.note: surface reading: an Englishman in his forties or fifties who writes travel guides
setter's reading: of the Middle Ages, a medieval poet who wrote of a pilgrimage

explanation.walkthrough: His Canterbury Tales follow pilgrims journeying from London to Canterbury, so he writes of travel.
explanation.definitionFit: The fourteenth-century poet wrote tales told by pilgrims on the road to Canterbury.

clue.text: Violent reaction against corporal punishment

blocks.note: first meaning: a strong hostile response against something
second, playful meaning: a stroke of the whip across the back

explanation.surface: Public outrage at the use of flogging.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is whimsical: split the word into a back and a lash.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp adverse reaction to an event or change is the everyday sense; the other is a whipping.

clue.text: Money for a horse

blocks.note: taken as written
a mount is a horse for riding

explanation.surface: Cash paid to buy a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum of cash is often called an amount, as in the amount owed on a bill.

clue.text: Frenzied woman made an error

indicators.note: an error puts things wrong, so the letters are put in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A woman in a frantic state has slipped up.
explanation.definitionFit: A female follower of Bacchus in Greek myth, given to ecstatic raving, hence any wildly frenzied woman.

clue.text: When indisposed, IÍd come to consult him

definitions.text: When indisposed, IÍd come to consult him

indicators.note: something indisposed is out of sorts, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A patient says that when unwell they would come and see him.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer while the middle words also supply its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor is the person a sick patient goes to see; this is an informal word for a physician.

clue.text: Pays a visit, after some persuasion?

blocks.note: first meaning: drops in at someone's home
second meaning: is won over to another view after argument

explanation.surface: Someone visits only after being talked into it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both calling at a house and changing one's mind to agree.

clue.text: A mistake whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: reading from either side gives the same result, so the word is the same both ways

blocks.note: a silly blunder

explanation.surface: An error, no matter how you view it.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for a foolish blunder, as in to make a bad gaffe.

clue.text: United Nations look into pre-Christian era

indicators.note: going into something places one item inside the other word

blocks.note: lo is an old exclamation meaning look
Before Christ

explanation.surface: The UN examines ancient history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United Nations' suggests the UN, but it means any group of countries that stand together.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of countries allied by common interest, such as a trading or voting alliance.

clue.text: They have small parts in a big picture

definitions.text: They have small parts in a big picture

blocks.clueFragment: They have small parts in a big picture
blocks.note: surface reading: bit-part actors in a major film

blocks.clueFragment: small parts in a big picture
blocks.note: setter's reading: small pictures or maps set within a larger one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Small parts in a big picture' sounds like minor film roles, but means little images placed inside a page.
explanation.definitionFit: Small maps or illustrations placed within the border of a larger one are called by this name.

clue.text: Shut up tight in the terminus

indicators.note: placing one word in another means it sits within that other word

blocks.note: close means tight, as in a close fit
a terminus is the end of a line

explanation.surface: Someone kept closely confined at the end of the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shut up within walls or a container is enclosed, a past participle like the definition.
